title: AFOOFT
description:
“Chicken Jump Into Your Mouth” How can you resist a dish like this? Easy to make, done quickly, and, most of all, delicious!
You can make this with or without a little cheese (like provolone) melted on top at the end, but only a little; you don’t want to interfere with the simple, but robust flavors.
START TO FINISH: 45 MIN
Chicken Saltimbocca
Heat oven to 200 degrees. Combine flour and 1 teaspoon pepper in shallow dish.
Slice thick cutlets horizontally (after firming them up in a freezer for a few minutes) or pound to ½ inch thick.
Pat cutlets dry with paper towels. Dredge chicken in flour, shaking off any excess. Lay cutlets flat and sprinkle evenly with minced sage. Place 1 prosciutto slice on top of each cutlet, pressing lightly to adhere; set aside.
Add half of cutlets to pan, prosciutto-side down, and cook until light golden brown, 2 to 3 minutes. Flip and cook on other side until light golden brown, about 2 minutes more.
Transfer to wire rack set on rimmed baking sheet and keep warm in oven.
Repeat with remaining 2 tablespoons oil and cutlets, then transfer to oven to keep warm while preparing
Heat 2 tablespoons oil in 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat until beginning to shimmer. Add sage leaves (if using) and cook until leaves begin to change color and are fragrant, about 15 to 20 seconds. Using slotted spoon or tongs, remove sage to paper towel-lined plate; reserve.
Pour off excess fat from skillet. Stir in wine and chicken broth, scraping up any browned bits, and simmer until reduced to about 3/4 cup, 5 to 7 minutes.
Stir in lemon juice. Turn heat to low and whisk in butter, 1 tablespoon at a time. Off heat, stir in parsley and season with salt and pepper.
Remove chicken from oven and place on platter. Spoon sauce over cutlets before serving.
directions: This is good with noodles or even garlic mashed potatoes – something to soak up the tasty sauce. Green vegetables are always good but you could have an oven-roasted tomato instead.
We first had this in the Fall of 1991, after the recipe appeared in The New York Times (from Jacques Pepin). It was so good – we thought of it as the “recipe of the year!”
Somehow, we lost the specific instructions but when Lauren was working at the PSU library, voila, she dug it up from old microfiches.
Don’t make this with canned tuna unless you absolutely have to.
Bring water (with a little salt) to boil in saucepan.
Peel the potatoes, if desired, and cut into small bit-sized pieces.
Boil until tender but still firm, 7-10 minutes. Drain and let cool.
Meanwhile, prepare the dressing. In a little electric mixer (or by hand), mix well together the mustard, garlic, vinegar, olive oil, and 1 tablespoon salt and 1 teaspoon pepper (or to taste).
Add the potatoes to the dressing.

Using the same water or a new pot of salted boiling water, boil the green beans 3 minutes (or less for haricot verts, or more for larger beans). Drain under cold water for a few seconds to stop the cooking and preserve the bright green color. Depending on the size, cut the beans for easy eating.
Peel the yellow (or red or orange) pepper as best you can with a vegetable peeler and cut into thin julienne strips.
Cut the tomatoes in half across the stem, squeeze out the seeds, and cut the unpeeled flesh into 1 inch pieces.
No more than 1 hour before serving, add the beans, pepper, onions, tomatoes, and olives to potatoes. Mix well.
Cut the tuna into 1 inch cubes.
When almost ready to serve, heat a large heavy skillet over high heat for 4 or 5 minutes, until very hot. Sprinkle the tuna liberally with black pepper and salt and then roll in the canola oil.
Place the tuna cubes in the hot skillet and saute over high heat for 2-3 minutes until they are lightly browned on the outside and cooked until rare on the inside.
To serve, line a large platter with the lettuce leaves. Mound the Salade Niçoise in the center of the platter and sprinkle the freshly cooked tuna and the basil leaves on top.
You don’t need much else with this besides some crusty bread and a nice wine (maybe a tasty Char- donnay). You might even follow up with a little cheese to round out this delicious dish.

According to Julia Child, Beef Bourguignon “is certainly one of the most delicious beef dishes concocted by man.” We certainly agree and are working from her recipe from “Mastering the Art of French Cooking,” the book that changed the way America cooks.
I got to eat with Julia once (I was her escort), at a dinner with Stan Calderwood, my boss at Trinity and a good friend of Julia’s. It was here that she taught me to enjoy a “very wet Martini.”
Beef Bourguignon is not only classic French but classic “comfort food.”

Saute the bacon in the oil over moderate heat for 3 to 5 minutes. Remove to a side dish, leaving the bacon fat in the pan.
Return the beef and bacon to the casserole with the vegetables and toss with a teaspoon of salt and some pepper. Then sprinkle on the 2 tablespoons of flour.

Set the casserole uncovered in the middle position of the preheated oven for 4 minutes. Toss the meat around and return to the oven for 4 minutes more. (This browns the flour and covers the meat with a light crust.)
Remove the casserole and turn the oven down to 325 degrees.
Stir in the wine and enough beef stock so that the meat is barely covered. Add the tomato paste, garlic, thyme, and bay leaf.
Bring to a simmer on top of the stove. Then cover the casserole and set in the lower third of the oven (now 325 degrees).
Regulate the heat so the liquid simmers very slowly for about 2 ½ hours. The meat should be fork tender.
Cut the beef into thick cubes, 1 to 2 inches, and dry with paper towels; it won’t brown if its damp.
Saute the beef, a few pieces at a time, in the hot oil and bacon fat until nicely browned on all sides, 5-7 minutes. Add the browned pieces to the bacon.
In the same fat, brown the chopped vegetables, 5-7 minutes. Pour out the sauteing fat.

I usually use frozen pearl onions because they’re peeled and ready to go. Add a splash of water and a little butter to a small pan and heat the onions over moderately high heat until the water evaporates and then the onions get a nice brown color, around 10 minutes.
When the beef is tender (about 2 ½ hours), carefully take the meat out in keep warm. Strain the casserole liquid through a sieve into a saucepan. Skim off any fat in the sauce.
You can pick on the casserole-cooked vegetables, grind them up and push some through a fine sieve, or toss them out.
Check the sauce for consistency – it should be silky and smooth – adding more broth or water if too thick or thickening it by boiling it down a bit. Also check for salt and pepper.
Add the sauteed vegetable to the sauce and heat. Then pour all over the beef.
Serve with potatoes or noodles, garnished with chopped parsley.

We used to go around town in New York City, looking for places that made Caesar Salad (not many) and who did the best job. Now every restaurant everywhere has this salad on the menu, but few do it well.
This is our favorite and it’s easy to prepare with a food processor.
And, of course, you can add to the basic salad grilled chicken, tuna, steak, etc.
With the now empty processor running, drop the garlic cloves in to finely mince them.
Add all the rest of dressing ingredients (not the lettuce, croutons, and cheese) to the food processor bowl.
Mix well until smooth, about 30 seconds.
Break up the cleaned Romaine to bite-sized pieces and add the dressing (not necessarily all depending on you tastes). Toss.
Add the croutons and cheese. Toss and serve.
If making your own croutons, cut up some good bread (could be a little stale) into little cubes of about ¼ - ½ inches on the sides.
Bake these in a 350 degree oven until lightly browned, about 15 minutes, stirring to turn occasionally.
With the food processor, finely grind the Parmesan cheese (you can save the extra for a few days if you’d like). Take the cheese out of the processor.
While the beef is cooking, saute the mushrooms in some butter until nicely browned, 7-10 minutes.
Similarly, saute the carrots in a little butter until browned, 7-10 minutes.
